draft.title: Neuroimaging
card: Neuroimaging uses scanning technology to look at a living brain without opening the skull. Different scans show different things.
CT and MRI show the brain's structure, which means its shape, size and any damage, such as a tumour or a injury.
PET and fMRI show which brain areas are active during a task, such as reading or moving a hand. They do this by detecting changes linked to activity, such as blood flow or the use of glucose.
Researchers use functional scans while people do tasks. This lets them link a function to a place in the brain.
draft.remember: Structural scans show what the brain looks like. Functional scans show what it is doing.

a.q: Which scan would best show which brain areas are active while a person solves a puzzle?
opts: fMRI
CT
MRI
A structural scan
a.why: fMRI is a functional scan, so it shows areas that are active during a task. CT and MRI show structure only, so they can show a brain's shape but not which areas are working on the puzzle.
a.clue: Look for a scan that shows activity, not just structure.

b.q: Dr Lee wants to see whether a patient's head injury has changed the size or shape of part of the brain. Which scan suits this, and why?
opts: MRI, because it shows the brain's structure
PET, because it shows the brain's structure
fMRI, because it shows the brain's structure
MRI, because it shows the brain's activity
b.why: MRI is a structural scan, so it can show changes in shape or size after an injury. PET and fMRI are functional scans that show activity, so they are not the best choice for checking structure.
b.clue: Size and shape are about structure, not activity.

b.best: MRI, because it shows the brain's structure
